summary: Describes a procedure for renumbering an IPv6 network from one prefix to another without a flag day. It uses the ability to give interfaces multiple addresses for a make-before-break transition and addresses naming and configuration issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving to a new address while keeping the old one active for a while means no mail gets lost. This memo explains how to do that for a whole network without a sudden switchover.

questions: how to renumber an ipv6 network
subtitle: Move to a new IPv6 address range without downtime

tldr.problem: Renumbering an IPv6 network from one prefix to another is inevitable but difficult: a traditional flag-day cutover causes service outage, and configurations are scattered across many systems and devices.
tldr.mechanism: The procedure uses IPv6's ability to assign multiple addresses to interfaces for a 'make-before-break' transition: the new prefix is deployed and tested while the old prefix remains active, allowing hosts to migrate at their own pace before the old prefix is decommissioned.
tldr.outcome: Networks can renumber without planned downtime if they carefully manage DNS, DHCP, configurations and application caches through a series of stable intermediate states.

facts.label: Transition states
facts.value: Eight stable states from old to new prefix

today: RFC 4192 remains informational guidance for IPv6 network administrators. It updates RFC 2072's earlier renumbering guidance to address IPv6-specific issues. The procedure is still used in practice, though organizations report that renumbering remains operationally difficult despite the make-before-break approach.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Networks must sometimes renumber from one IPv6 prefix to another. A change of Internet service provider, a provider's prefix change, or an organization's own address policy change can trigger renumbering. The challenge is that a traditional flag day (a planned outage in which the change happens suddenly) is disruptive. This document describes a procedure to renumber using a make-before-break approach: the new prefix is deployed and tested while the old prefix remains operational, allowing the network to reach a stable state with both prefixes in use before transitioning to the new prefix alone.

The procedure is straightforward in theory but operationally difficult: addresses are embedded in routing configurations, firewalls, access control lists, applications, DNS records, DHCP servers, and static configuration files. Automating the discovery and update of all these places is challenging, and the procedure must be tailored to each network environment.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network changes its address range, it can either shut down for a day and switch over (flag day), or it can make the new range available first while keeping the old one working, then gradually move everyone to the new one. The second way is better but takes planning.

sections.title: Detailed Renumbering Procedure
sections.content: The procedure moves the network through eight states, each stable, until the transition completes. Initially the network uses only the old prefix. The first steps prepare the network infrastructure for the new prefix without using it for data forwarding: link prefixes are assigned, routes are added, and firewalls and access control lists are updated for the new prefix in parallel with the old. Once infrastructure is ready and tested, host addresses from the new prefix are assigned while old addresses are retained. DNS is updated for the new prefix, and hosts begin using new addresses. A period of stable operation with both prefixes in use follows, allowing applications time to transition. DNS records for the old prefix are then redirected or removed, and old prefix addresses are phased out through TTL management. Finally, the old prefix is removed from routing and static configurations, and the network reaches a stable state using only the new prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The process has clear steps: prepare the new infrastructure, add new addresses to hosts, let both work side-by-side, gradually shift traffic to the new addresses, then clean up the old ones.

sections.title: Managing DNS, DHCP and Configuration
sections.content: DNS Time-to-Live (TTL) values and DHCP lease times control how quickly the network can transition. Before renumbering, TTL values for affected records should be lowered to speed propagation of changes; DHCP T1 parameters (the time at which a host re-contacts the server) may be reduced; and DHCP Reconfigure messages can trigger hosts to request new addresses immediately. Dynamic DNS (DDNS) allows hosts to update their own records, but inter-administrative domain trust relationships must be established in advance, especially for reverse-zone updates. Applications may cache DNS responses or IP addresses indefinitely, necessitating either tool development to flush caches or manual intervention on affected systems. Static configuration in routers, switches and service devices must be discovered and updated methodically, often requiring automated tools to map old addresses to new ones and update configuration files.
sections.plainLanguage: Many services hold onto old addresses. You control how long with DNS TTLs and DHCP timers. You must find and update static addresses in configuration files, and some applications will stubbornly remember old addresses until you restart them.

sections.title: Operational Hazards and Prevention
sections.content: Several operational pitfalls complicate renumbering. Applications may ignore DNS TTLs and continue using stale cached addresses. Voice over IP phones, dedicated manufacturing devices, and other equipment with static bootstrap configurations may not contact a DHCP server or reconsult DNS, requiring manual intervention. BGP routers are particularly sensitive: if one end of a BGP peering uses the new address while the other uses the old, the connection is broken. BGP should be brought up on the new address before the old is removed. Ingress filtering policies at network edges may block traffic during the transition if not updated carefully. Link flaps in BGP can cause routing instability if address transitions are not coordinated between peers. Devices should use domain names for configuration rather than static IP addresses, and should re-resolve names periodically rather than only at startup.
sections.plainLanguage: Old devices and services might get stuck with the old address. Special attention is needed for BGP routers (which peer with each other) and edge firewalls that filter traffic.
